article.headline: How Agent Skills and a Plan File Beat the Fifteen-Minute Limit
article.lede: AI coding agents routinely stall mid-task — not from inability, but from a structural constraint: the context window fills, the model loses track of earlier decisions, and the session fragments across multiple conversations. Developer DimitriGilbert's answer ties together three elements: a reusable orchestration skill from the skills.sh ecosystem, strict role separation among sub-agents, and a plan committed to disk before execution begins. The combination reportedly sustains coding sessions of four hours or more without human prompting.
article.body:
The underlying bottleneck is the **context window** — the fixed-size token buffer an AI model can process at once. Claude Code's window holds up to 200,000 tokens, which sounds generous until a complex agentic session begins reading files, running tool calls, and accumulating reasoning traces. At roughly 83 percent capacity, Claude Code triggers automatic *context compaction*: it summarises the session to make room. That summary discards precise architectural decisions, file states, and progress tracking — the exact information a long-running agent needs to stay coherent. In practice, users routinely hit this wall in fifteen to twenty minutes.

The workflow begins with *agent skills* — reusable instruction sets distributed through skills.sh, a directory and CLI launched by Vercel in January 2026. Skills follow an open specification now maintained across 54 compatible coding agents: each is a folder containing a SKILL.md file with natural-language instructions. The agent holds names and descriptions in context at all times but fetches full instructions only when a relevant task arises, keeping baseline overhead low. DimitriGilbert's ai-skills repository on GitHub contributes a pair of complementary skills: `subagent-planificator` (which has specialist sub-agents collaborate on a plan) and `subagent-orchestration` (which executes it).

The orchestration skill imposes strict role separation. An orchestrator coordinates three types of worker: *implementers* write code, *validators* read it line-by-line and run automated checks, and *fixers* resolve whatever validation finds. The orchestrator never writes code itself. Each worker runs in an isolated context window, so a sub-agent reading dozens of files does not contaminate the coordinator's session. The user approves the plan once at the start; after that the orchestrator manages the implementer-validator-fixer loop autonomously, retrying failed steps up to a fixed limit.

The plan file is what makes repeated context resets cheap. Rather than holding the plan in the conversation, the workflow writes it to a markdown file on disk before execution begins. When the context overflows — as it inevitably will on a several-hour task — the user starts a new conversation. The fresh session loads the skill, reads the plan file, and resumes from the precise stopping point. What was previously a frustrating interruption becomes a seamless checkpoint.

The tweet's reference to *GLM* points to the model family from Zhipu AI, a Chinese AI lab that operates internationally under the brand Z.ai. The subagent-orchestration pattern is model-agnostic: Claude Code's interface can be pointed at Zhipu AI's API instead of Anthropic's, substituting GLM as the inference backend. GLM-4.7, released in December 2025, scores 73.8 percent on *SWE-bench* — a benchmark measuring autonomous resolution of real GitHub software engineering issues — putting it near Claude Sonnet territory at a substantially lower monthly cost. DimitriGilbert ran the full four-hour session on GLM, suggesting the technique is not restricted to any one provider.

concepts.definition: The fixed-size token buffer an LLM can process at one time. For Claude Code, this is 200,000 tokens — large, but one that fills quickly when an agent reads many files, runs tool calls, and accumulates reasoning traces across a long session. Once full, the model cannot receive new input without discarding prior content.

An automatic process Claude Code triggers when the context window approaches capacity (around 83 percent full). It summarises the session history to make room for new tokens. Helpful for short tasks; costly for long ones, because compaction discards precise architectural decisions, file states, and progress tracking that the agent built up earlier in the session.

Reusable instruction sets — each a folder containing a SKILL.md file with natural-language instructions — that extend an AI coding agent's capabilities. Skills load lazily: the agent holds brief descriptions in context at all times but fetches full instructions only when a matching task arises. An open specification maintained across 54+ compatible agents and distributed through Vercel's skills.sh directory.

A pattern in which a coordinating agent dispatches tasks to specialised sub-agents, each running in its own isolated context window. The coordinator receives only the sub-agent's final output — not its internal reasoning history — keeping the main session clean and enabling multi-hour workflows that would otherwise exhaust a single agent's memory.

A benchmark that measures how often an LLM can autonomously resolve real GitHub software engineering issues: find the bug, write a correct patch, pass the test suite. Widely used as a more meaningful proxy for practical coding ability than synthetic code-generation tests, because it requires understanding existing codebases rather than generating isolated snippets.

A markdown file written to disk at the start of an agentic session, serving as persistent working memory. Because it lives on the filesystem rather than in the conversation, it survives context resets. When a session overflows and a new conversation begins, the agent reads the plan file and resumes from the exact stopping point — making resets a minor inconvenience rather than a project failure.

repos.summary: A collection of 18+ specialised skills for AI coding agents including Claude Code and OpenCode. The subagent-orchestration skill implements a strict implementer/validator/fixer triad in which the orchestrating agent never writes code itself, enabling autonomous multi-phase development with retry loops. Its companion subagent-planificator skill uses multiple specialist agents to collaboratively produce a structured plan before execution begins.

The open-source CLI and directory powering the skills.sh Agent Skills ecosystem. Provides commands to search, install, and manage skills across 54+ compatible AI coding agents. The repository underpins the community infrastructure for discovering and distributing reusable agent instruction sets.
